title: Guessing Candies in a Jar
question: How can you estimate something you cannot fully count?
hook: A glass jar, a quick look, and a number you can defend.
idea: A good estimate projects from what you can see, and balances being precise enough to use against being so precise it is likely wrong.

beats.prompt: You can see 50 candies through the glass, and the jar looks about 20 times larger than the part holding them. What single guess for the total makes sense?

choices.label: About 50, only the ones you can see
choices.feedback: The visible candies are only part of the jar, so the total must be larger.

choices.label: About 70, a little more than visible
choices.feedback: A jar 20 times larger than the visible part should hold far more than that.

beats.explain: Projecting 50 visible candies across a volume about 20 times larger suggests about a thousand. That single best guess is called a point estimate.

pairs: A single value believed closest to the actual one
A wide range that can be too broad to help
The rule that turns data into an estimate
beats.explain: These are three words for the pieces of estimating: a single best guess, a range, and the rule that produces them.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: I can see 50 candies through the glass.
The jar looks about 20 times larger than the part I counted.
So my best single guess is about 1,000 candies.
So there are certainly exactly 1,000 candies.
beats.explain: A point estimate is likely to be incorrect, because the number of visible candies is too small to be sure it has no anomalies that differ from the rest of the jar.

beats.prompt: You predict 300 guests will come to a party, but only 250 do. What was your estimate?

choices.label: An underestimate
choices.feedback: An underestimate falls short of the actual result; yours was higher.

choices.label: Neither, because estimates are never compared with results
choices.feedback: An estimate is called over or under by comparing it with the actual result.

beats.explain: An estimate that exceeds the actual result is an overestimate; one that falls short is an underestimate.
